The bill repeals schedules for historical events.

This bill would create a new parliamentary committee to oversee Australia's defence agencies.
The committee would have up to 13 members and could request information, documents, and briefings, but would be restricted from publicly disclosing sensitive information without ministerial approval.
The bill includes criminal offences for unauthorised use or disclosure of protected information by committee members, their staff, and other authorised parliamentarians.
Creates the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Defence within the Defence Act 1903.
Gives the committee power to review, monitor, and report on Australian defence agencies, excluding certain intelligence organisations.
Imposes restrictions on public proceedings and disclosure of protected information, with ministerial certificates overriding disclosure requirements.
Establishes criminal offences for unauthorised use or disclosure of protected information.

Australian defence agencies, including the Australian Defence Force, Department of Defence, and Department of Veterans' Affairs, as well as committee members, their staff, and other authorised parliamentarians.

The bill would let the Administrative Review Tribunal decide some cases without holding an oral hearing, and would require it to decide certain student visa and temporary visa reviews on the papers.

It would amend the Administrative Review Tribunal Act 2024 to give the tribunal a new discretion to skip oral hearings when issues can be adequately determined in writing and parties have had a chance to comment.

The bill would also amend the Migration Act 1958 to require the tribunal to decide student visa refusal reviews and other prescribed temporary visa reviews without an oral hearing, using a new written review procedure.
Expands the circumstances in which the tribunal may decide a proceeding without an oral hearing.
Requires the tribunal to decide certain student visa and temporary visa reviews on the papers without an oral hearing.
Inserts a new discretion into section 106 of the Administrative Review Tribunal Act 2024.
Creates a new Division 4A of Part 5 of the Migration Act 1958 for paper-based reviews.
Applicants for review of student visa refusals and certain temporary visa decisions, and parties to proceedings before the Administrative Review Tribunal.

This bill would set statutory minimum staffing levels for parliamentarians who are not part of the government, and prevent the executive from lowering those levels later.
It would entrench these minimums in the Members of Parliament (Staff) Act 1984, with the Prime Minister allowed to raise but not reduce them through determinations.
Opposition parties would get the larger of 110 personal staff or 22 percent of the government's allocation, while other non-government groups get smaller guaranteed numbers.
The bill would guarantee minimum staffing entitlements in three categories: opposition, other non-government parliamentarians, and independents or minority party members.
It would remove the executive's power to reduce those minima by later determination.
It would clarify that the Prime Minister may only increase these minimum entitlements.
Non-government parliamentarians, including opposition parties, minor parties, and independents, are affected.
